# Compatible support arrays and a Minkowski-depth obstruction

## 1. An exact cone description

Fix a finite lattice-convex P. For z in P let

    L_z={lambda>=0: sum_w lambda_w=1, sum_w lambda_w w=z}.

These are finite-dimensional compact polytopes. Their vertices have support
on at most r+1 affinely independent points, where r=dim aff(P): otherwise a
nonzero affine dependence permits a two-sided perturbation of the positive
coefficients and contradicts extremality.

Suppose h_z is the support function of a nonempty compact convex K_z. The
family is an ACTUAL compatible convex fiber family exactly when

    h_z(u) >= sum_w lambda_w h_w(u)

for every z, every u, and every vertex lambda of L_z. Necessity is convexity.
For sufficiency, the vertex inequalities imply all barycentric inequalities
by convex combination. They say that every Minkowski combination of the
fibers with integer-coordinate barycenter z is contained in K_z. Grouping
terms in an arbitrary convex combination proves that the fiber of the convex
hull at z has no additional points.

Thus compatible support arrays form a closed convex cone under pointwise
addition and nonnegative scaling. These operations correspond to FIBERWISE
Minkowski addition and continuous-coordinate dilation. They are not ambient
Minkowski addition, which would also add the integer coordinates.

If P has an interior integer point z_0, the lineality consists precisely of
arrays h_z(u)=u.(Bz+b). Indeed, if h and -h both belong to the cone, every
fiber has width zero and is a point c_z. Fixed strictly positive barycentric
weights at z_0, and their small perturbations along every affine dependence,
force all affine-dependence sums of the c_z to vanish. Hence c_z=Bz+b.
The converse is immediate.

For a fixed complete simplicial fan in continuous normal space, arrays that
are linear on each cone of the fan form a FINITE polyhedral cone. Support
convexity is finitely many linear inequalities: the linear piece of any
maximal cone must lie below the specified values on every fan ray. The
compatibility inequalities need be checked only on those rays because all
terms are linear on each fan cone. This provides an exact finite tangent
cone for simultaneous support perturbations; there is no independent-fiber
compatibility approximation here.

## 2. Maximum depth is not quasiconcave on this cone

Take n=d=1 and P={0,1,2,3}. Let A and B have interval fibers

    z      A_z          B_z
    0      [0,12]       [0,21]
    1      [-3,24]      [-9,24]
    2      [-1,28]      [-3,21]
    3      [6,32]       [7,14].

They are actual convex fiber families. The successive lower-endpoint slopes
are (-3,2,7) and (-9,6,10), both increasing; the upper-endpoint slopes are
(12,4,4) and (3,-3,-7), both decreasing. Their fiberwise Minkowski sum D has
fibers

    [0,33], [-12,48], [-4,49], [13,46].

Their masses are M_A=94, M_B=85, M_D=179. Exact depth calculations give

    depth_A((2,14))=20/47,
    depth_B((1,33/4))=147/340,
    maxdepth(D)=63/179.

Thus

    maxdepth(A+B) < min{maxdepth(A), maxdepth(B)}.

Only the displayed LOWER bounds for A and B are needed; no claim about the
locations of their other maximizers is required.

Here is a complete finite verification method for the claimed point depths.
At a point (k,x), a nonvertical halfspace through that point is bounded by

    y=x+a(z-k).

Its above-line mass is a continuous piecewise-affine function of a. Its
breakpoints are exactly a=(e-x)/(j-k), where e is an endpoint of a different
fiber j. Therefore its minimum and maximum occur at these finitely many
breakpoints or at the limits a tending to plus or minus infinity. Checking
both orientations at these values covers EVERY oblique halfspace. The
vertical halfspaces contain an entire candidate fiber and can be checked
separately. This calculation yields the three displayed point values; the
rational verifier below executes every breakpoint and both infinite limits.

For a short global upper certificate on D, split each fiber at the following
x-value and use the two indicated fixed lines. Take the halfspace BELOW the
first line for x at or below the split, and ABOVE the second line otherwise:

    z=0, split 33/2:
        y=33/2-100z,       y=33/2+100z;          each mass 33/2.
    z=1, split 18:
        y=40-22z,          y=31z-13;            each mass 63.
    z=2, split 45/2:
        y=(69z-93)/2,      y=(147-51z)/2;       each mass 119/2.
    z=3, split 59/2:
        y=59/2+100(z-3),   y=59/2-100(z-3);     each mass 33/2.

These eight closed caps cover D pointwise and all have mass at most 63.
The point (1,18) has depth 63/179 by the complete slope calculation, proving
the exact maximum for D.

The obstruction survives CENTRAL UNIT-VOLUME normalization. Both A/27 and
B/33 have their fiber at z=1 of length one, and

    (27/60)(A/27)+(33/60)(B/33)=(A+B)/60.

Continuous-coordinate scaling preserves normalized depths. Hence the failure
occurs on the same compact normalized fixed-P class used for extremal
attainment, not merely through a change in normalization.

The exact Fraction script `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_minkowski_depth_obstruction.py` checks
compatibility, every required halfspace minimum, all eight cap masses, and
the normalized convex-combination identity. It passes. This rules out an
extreme-ray reduction based on quasiconcavity of maximum depth; it does not
rule out a different first-order variational argument.
